items.title: Similar is more than the same general shape
items.student: Use these complete descriptions. A andB are right triangles with corresponding side lengths(3,4,5) and(6,8,10). RectanglesC,D,E have sides2by3,4by6 and4by5 respectively,all angles90°. A rhombusF has four sides2and angles60°,120°,60°,120°;squareG has four sides2and four right angles. Decide which specified pairs A/B,C/D,C/E,F/G are similar. Give a correspondence,common positive length ratio and angle reason where appropriate.
items.teacher: A/B similar with factor2 and corresponding right-triangle shapes;the three proportional side lengths establish triangle similarity. C/D similar with factor2 and equal corresponding angles. C/E not similar because side ratios2and5/3 disagree. F/G not similar despite side ratio1 because angles differ. Similarity requires matching corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths;equal areas,volumes or a vague outline alone do not prove it.

items.title: Find a centre from matching vertices
items.student: Under one nonidentity enlargement,triangleA(2,1),B(4,1),C(2,3) maps toA′(3,1),B′(7,1),C′(3,5). Draw equal-unit perpendicular axes and plot all six points. Extend linesAA′ andCC′ to their intersection O;check BB′ passes through it. Find the image/object ratio of corresponding lengths and compare directed centre-to-point distances. Label the centre and linear scale factor. If no squared paper is supplied,draw axes with0.5cm per coordinate unit using a ruler.
items.teacher: AA′ lies ony=1;CC′ lies ony=2x−1;intersectionO(1,1). BB′ also lies ony=1. AB=2,A′B′=4,sofactor2. OA′=2OA,OB′=2OB,OC′=2OC on the same rays. Check every pair,not only one point. For factor1,the identity has no uniquely determined centre;the given data deliberately use factor2.

items.title: Construct a positive enlargement
items.student: Use equal coordinate scales,one unit0.5cm on paper. O(0,0) is the centre;triangleP(1,1),Q(3,1),R(1,2) has scale factor2. Draw rays from O through each vertex and locate each image at twice its original centre distance. Join and label the image. Independently check with coordinates and compare corresponding side lengths and angles. Explain why simply adding2to every coordinate is a different transformation.
items.teacher: P′(2,2),Q′(6,2),R′(2,4). Corresponding lengths double and angles are preserved. On plain paper,the ray construction uses the same stated coordinates and ruler distances;on the Cartesian plane,the coordinate rule agrees. Adding(2,2) would translate points and would sendQto(5,3),not(6,2). An enlargement scales each centre-to-point displacement,not a fixed additive offset.

items.title: A reduction away from the origin
items.student: CentreO(2,1),scale factor1/2;triangleP(4,3),Q(8,3),R(4,7). Plot the original and place each image halfway from O to its vertex. Record image coordinates and verify each centre-to-point distance ratio. Explain why halving the original coordinates alone would give the wrong result. Use equal coordinate scales and a labelled centre.
items.teacher: P′(3,2),Q′(5,2),R′(3,4). Compute each coordinate as centre coordinate plus half the difference from the centre. HalvingP’s coordinates would give(2,1.5),not the correct image(3,2). A factor between0and1 gives a reduction;it still preserves corresponding angles and multiplies lengths by the positive factor.

items.title: A negative coordinate factor and physical lengths
items.student: On equal-unit axes,enlargeP(1,1),Q(3,1),R(1,2) aboutO(0,0) with signed factor−2. Draw the opposite rays and locate all images. Compare a corresponding side’s positive length ratio and the signed coordinate factor. Is this a reflection in a line? Explain why neither an area nor a volume becomes negative. State what factors0and1 would do.
items.teacher: P′(−2,−2),Q′(−6,−2),R′(−2,−4). Positive length ratio is|−2|=2. This planar map is a180°turn plus a positive enlargement,not a line reflection;the boundary’s clockwise/counterclockwise order is preserved. Physical areas scale by|k|²=4 and volumes by|k|³=8 for similar solids. Factor0 collapses everything toO and is not a nondegenerate similarity;factor1 is the identity with no unique centre. Main physical scale ratios below are positive,not signed.

items.title: Area follows two length directions
items.student: Compare similar rectangles3cmby2cm and9cmby6cm. Compute their areas,the common length ratio and the area ratio. Compare triangles with base4cm,height3cm and their factor2images with base8cm,height6cm. Also compare total surface areas of cubes with edges2cm and6cm. Derive why a positive length ratio k gives area ratio k²,including surface areas of geometrically similar solids.
items.teacher: Rectangles6cm²and54cm²,k=3,area ratio9. Triangles6cm²and24cm²,k=2,area ratio4. Cubes surface6×2²=24cm²and6×6²=216cm²,ratio9. Two independent length factors multiply in an area formula;similar curved/plane surfaces obey the same scaling principle. These conclusions require genuine geometric similarity and corresponding measures,not merely two arbitrary equal-area figures.

items.title: Volume follows three length directions
items.student: Compare cubes with edges2cm and6cm,then similar cuboids2cmby3cmby4cm and6cmby9cmby12cm. Find both volumes and their ratios,and relate them to the common positive length ratio. A cube2cmperedge and a cuboid1cmby2cmby4cm both have volume8cm³:does equality of volume make them similar? Explain.
items.teacher: Cubes8cm³and216cm³,ratio27,k=3. Cuboids24cm³and648cm³,ratio27,k=3. Three independent length factors multiply,so volume ratio k³. The cube and1×2×4cuboid are not similar:corresponding side ratios cannot all agree. Equal volume alone does not justify applying a similarity scale law. Keep cm³different from cm²and cm.

items.title: Recover a length ratio from area or volume
items.student: For geometrically similar figures with small-to-large area ratio4:25,find the positive large/small length ratio. For similar solids with small-to-large volume ratio8:125,find the same length ratio and corresponding area ratio. For a positive length ratio3,relate length,area and volume ratios. Explain why the assumption of similarity and the chosen ratio direction must be stated.
items.teacher: Area case k=√(25/4)=5/2. Volume case k=cube root(125/8)=5/2;area ratio large/small25/4. For k3,the ratios large/small are3,9,27. Reverse directions give1/3,1/9,1/27. If an enlargement uses a negative signed coordinate factor,the physical length ratio is its magnitude;physical volume is not k³with a negative sign. Area or volume ratios alone do not establish similarity.

items.title: A model scale needs unit checks
items.student: A fictional rectangular model is4cmby6cm at scale1:50,meaning1modelcm represents50actualcm in every length direction. Find actual dimensions in metres,the model area in cm²,the actual area in m² and the actual/model area ratio after using the same area units. Explain why multiplying the model area by50 alone fails. No actual building,site visit or measurement is implied.
items.teacher: Actual200cmby300cm=2mby3m;model area24cm²;actual60000cm²=6m²;area ratio2500=50². Multiplying24cm²by50 gives1200cm²,not the correct area. Use matching units before forming ratios. State the idealised rectangle and uniform scale assumptions;do not claim the numbers are a real site survey.

items.title: Design two similar learning models
items.student: Project design stage only. Plan two ideal closed paper cubes with target edge lengths2cm and4cm. For each cube,draw a net of six equal squares:use cell positions(row0,col1),(row1,col0),(row1,col1),(row1,col2),(row2,col1),(row3,col1). Each cell is one face with the target edge length;rows run downward,columns rightward. The four cells incol1 form a vertical strip,and the extra two attach left/right of its second cell. Add optional small fastening tabs outside faces without changing face dimensions. Label target lengths and calculate ideal surface area and volume for each. List clean reused paper/card,ruler,pencil and teacher-approved fastening/precutting provision. A plan is not a completed model. State the large/small length,area and volume scale factors and explain their relationship.
items.teacher: This is a valid six-square cube net. Small surface24cm²,volume8cm³;large surface96cm²,volume64cm³;length ratio2,area ratio4,volume ratio8. Large net face extent12cmwide by16cmhigh before tabs fits a standard A4sheet;draw to the stated dimensions rather than assuming a displayed diagram’s print scale. Teacher may prepare identical fully dimensioned nets from these instructions. Actual cutting/folding resources and safe access are confirmed before the next lesson;the design alone does not complete the source making activity.

items.title: Make and check the cube pair honestly
items.student: Only after teacher preparation/approval,use the CSE10nets to fold and fasten the two models. Teacher provides safely precut nets or supervises blunt scissors;no knives,hot glue or staples. Mark faces and corresponding edges,check actual edge lengths with a ruler and record the measurements and any deviations from the ideal targets. Compare the ideal length/area/volume ratios with what the target models represent;do not claim exact measured similarity if construction errors disagree. Each learner records their own contribution and actual completed/not completed status. If making resources are unavailable,complete the paper analysis and mark the actual project NOT OBSERVED.
items.teacher: The intended models have k2,area ratio4 andvolume ratio8. Closed six-face shapes must correspond to the specified nets,with fastening tabs outside face areas. Actual measurements/status are learner/teacher observations,not invented data. Small construction differences make measured ratios approximate;use ideal targets for exact calculations and report deviations separately. Responsibility and integrity include caring for clean materials and reporting actual dimensions/status honestly. Real volume is not measured by filling the paper models.

items.title: Audit the scale argument and its usefulness
items.student: Individually repair: A doubling every length doubles area and volume; B a signed coordinate factor−2 gives negative volume; C equal volumes prove two solids similar; D the model area in CSE9scales by50rather than2500. Give a checked numerical example or condition for each. Write a short reasoned statement explaining one useful scale decision from this unit and one limitation or assumption. A reasoned preference for an alternative method is accepted;enthusiasm is not graded. Then compare corrections respectfully with a peer if directed.
items.teacher: A area factor4,volume factor8;B physical ratios use|k|,so volume factor8;C CSE7cube/cuboid counterexample disproves it;D actual/model area ratio2500with matching units. Useful decisions may concern model dimensions,school learning models or area/volume planning,provided the numeric evidence and similarity/unit assumptions are correct. The written explanation supplies its own evidence;actual sharing and actual project completion remain separate.

items.title: Independent final scale data
items.student: Use only this final card and separate prompts. Under one nonidentity enlargement,matched verticesA(2,1),B(2,3) have imagesA′(3,1),B′(3,5). A separate triangleP(2,2),Q(6,2),R(2,4) is enlarged aboutO(0,0) with factor1/2. Similar cuboids have dimensions2cm,3cm,4cm and4cm,6cm,8cm. A separate pair of similar solids has total surface areas9cm²and225cm². Similar-solid small/large volumes are8cm³and27cm³. A fictional4cmby6cmrectangle model uses scale1:50in matching length units. Use equal-scale axes drawn with ruler if no grid is supplied. No teaching cards,peer consultation or worked keys.
items.teacher: I1:AA′liney1 andBB′liney2x−1 intersectat(1,1),length ratioA′B′/AB=4/2=2. Separate triangle imagesP′(1,1),Q′(3,1),R′(1,2). I2:cuboid surfaces52cm²and208cm²,ratio4;volumes24cm³and192cm³,ratio8;length ratio2. I3:area ratio225/9=25giveslength ratio5andvolume ratio125;volume ratio27/8giveslength ratio3/2andarea ratio9/4. I4:actual2mby3m,area6m²,matching-unit area ratio2500. Advice must link a checked result to a specific useful decision and state similarity,units/precision or model assumptions. No paper answer certifies an unobserved construction project.
